title: Program-Verifiable Evaluation for Temporal QA: Metrics for Evidence Validity
research_question: How can temporal question-answering systems be evaluated so that answer correctness is separated from whether the cited evidence was actually valid at the query time?
methodology: The paper defines a program-verifiable temporal-QA framework in which each question has a query time and each evidence document has an explicit validity interval. It introduces an oracle-answer diagnostic that fixes answers to gold while evaluating evidence selection, together with Recency-Aware Score, Recency-Aware Recall, Temporal Mismatch Rate, and evidence-attribution metrics. Evaluation uses the synthetic TimeFact-CEO benchmark and the semi-structured Wikidata-CEO corpus, comparing BM25, date and recency heuristics, and a lightweight lexico-temporal reranker. The paper additionally reports end-to-end evaluation, cross-corpus robustness, parameter sensitivity, and error analysis.

key_findings.finding: Answer correctness does not guarantee valid evidence: under oracle answers on TimeFact-CEO, 11.8 percent of selected citations are temporally invalid, with TMR 0.118 and RAS 0.903.
The proposed lexico-temporal reranker raises temporal-validity recall on TimeFact-CEO from 48.2 percent for BM25 to 88.2 percent, a 40.0 percentage-point improvement under oracle-answer evaluation.

On the noisy Wikidata-CEO corpus, the temporal reranker achieves RAS 0.936, RAR 0.934, and TMR 0.066, indicating that interval-aware evaluation remains useful outside the perfectly controlled synthetic benchmark.

First-stage retrieval coverage is the dominant bottleneck: coverage is 76.3 percent at K=3 and the authors attribute 82.4 percent of analyzed errors to gold evidence being absent from the retrieved candidate set.
Separating an oracle-answer diagnostic from end-to-end QA exposes evidence-timeliness failures that aggregate answer accuracy can hide.
The framework does not evaluate completeness of multi-document evidence because its primary protocol intentionally enforces a single top-1 evidence citation.

The evaluation covers changing temporal validity but does not establish generalization to unrestricted free-form multi-source generation, because experiments are confined to CEO-tenure facts with explicit intervals.

limitations: The framework assumes that evidence units have explicit validity intervals; purely implicit temporal signals require additional temporal grounding.
The minimum-citation policy evaluates one selected evidence document and therefore does not address multi-evidence synthesis or multi-hop temporal reasoning.
The main baselines are interpretable lexical, date, and recency heuristics rather than stronger neural or LLM-based temporal rerankers.
Both benchmarks use CEO-tenure facts, so cross-domain generalization remains unvalidated.
The framework evaluates evidence timeliness and attribution but not whether all decision-relevant evidence has been retrieved or summarized.
Its deterministic interval setting is substantially simpler than versioned free-form sources whose validity periods are uncertain or implicit.
raw_claims: A factually correct answer can still be supported by evidence that was invalid at the time referenced by the question.
The oracle-answer diagnostic fixes answer accuracy so evidence-timeliness errors can be measured independently.
RAS, RAR, and TMR quantify complementary aspects of temporal evidence validity.
TimeFact-CEO provides controlled synthetic validity intervals, whereas Wikidata-CEO contains noisier real-world interval data.
The lexico-temporal reranker substantially improves temporal evidence selection over lexical BM25 retrieval.
Retrieval coverage at K=3 is a major source of downstream evidence-selection error.
The framework uses exactly one cited evidence document in its minimum-citation evaluation protocol.
The experiments are restricted to CEO-tenure information with explicit validity intervals.
The paper references a public TimeFact-CEO code repository.
